## The four o’clock toast

I finished my last night shift on Sunday morning. Saturday, nine at night to half past seven in the morning, in majors. Fourteen years of nights, and that was the last one.

From Monday I’m on the days-only rota. This is good news. My knees think so. My GP, who has stopped finding my blood pressure remotely amusing, thinks so. I am hoping my sleep will eventually agree, once it has worked out what I’m asking of it.

I thought I would feel uncomplicatedly pleased.

Instead, I’ve been trying to write this and finding that it comes out either as an obituary or as another complaint about the NHS. Neither is quite what I mean. Nobody has died in this particular story. I am changing my working hours, not leaving emergency medicine. And I’ve written enough about staffing on this blog to last us all a while.

Still. Fourteen years is a long time to do something to your body and then suddenly stop.

***

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. I can’t reliably remember what I had for lunch yesterday, but I remember the frost on the windscreen during that first winter.

I was in the car park at the Infirmary, crying because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose of medication. I had. I checked, and I had. But the reassurance didn’t immediately reach the part of me that was sitting in the car, too tired to drive and too frightened to go home.

The frost is what has stayed. That, and the horrible effort of trying to make my own memory answer a straightforward question.

I don’t want to turn that younger version of me into a lesson about resilience. She was exhausted. She needed sleep. She did not need the experience to be character-building.

But she went back, and somewhere along the way nights became familiar. I learned what I could eat at two in the morning without regretting it. I learned that there is a kind of tiredness which makes every minor inconvenience feel like a personal attack. I learned, not always gracefully, to notice when that was happening and keep it out of my voice.

I also learned who would notice before I did.

Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing this for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs. I offer this fact without further comment, except to say that my knees would like it taken into account.

There is a particular comfort in working with people who know what you sound like when you’re reaching the end of yourself. You don’t have to announce it. Sometimes someone simply puts a mug beside you, or tells you to sit down for five minutes, in a tone that makes it clear this is not a discussion.

I will miss that. I will miss being known in that particular way.

***

People often imagine nights in emergency medicine as a succession of dramatic events. There are dramatic events, of course. There are things that require you to move very quickly, and things you carry home despite every effort not to.

But much of the work is less cinematic.

It is explaining something again because the first explanation didn’t get through. Finding a blanket. Checking something you’re fairly sure you’ve already checked. Remembering that the person asking you the same question has not had the benefit of hearing your answer to six other people.

Mostly, it is trying to stay kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

I haven’t always managed it. I’ve been brisk when I should have been patient. I’ve heard my own voice and wished I could take it back. Fatigue makes your world very small if you let it. You become preoccupied with the next job, the next interruption, how long it has been since you sat down.

Then someone does something that brings you back.

An older man once held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. There was nothing I could usefully say to that. I stayed for a moment. He went home later, which I was glad to hear.

I don’t know whether he would remember it. I do.

***

At four in the morning, someone makes toast.

Nobody admits to starting this. You become aware of the smell, and then there is toast in the staff room. Sometimes you get there while it’s still hot. Sometimes you don’t get there at all. Sometimes someone has saved you a piece.

Four o’clock toast is not particularly good toast. The circumstances are doing a fair amount of the work. But I have eaten it with people after difficult hours, and during ordinary ones, and while laughing at things which would not survive being repeated in daylight.

It is one of the things I keep thinking about now that I’ve finished.

Nights are where the department has often felt most itself to me. There are fewer managers about, though I don’t think that explains all of it. There is less room for ceremony. People are more direct. In my experience, they are often kinder too.

I don’t mean that daytime colleagues are less kind, or that nights have some exclusive claim on proper medicine. Only that there is a closeness to working through those hours together. You see people tired, worried, funny, occasionally unreasonable. They see you the same way. You get on with the work.

After fourteen years, that is a lot to step away from.

***

It has cost something, though.

My sister is in Bangalore. I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies, even on video, because of nights. She never once complained. I’m grateful for that, and I still wish I had been there.

There have been plenty of smaller absences. Things I technically could have attended, if I hadn’t needed to sleep. Conversations I was too tired to follow properly. Days off spent recovering, followed by the peculiar indignation of being back at work already.

For years, I treated this as a matter of organisation. If I slept at the right time, planned better, got the food and the curtains and the journey home right, perhaps I could make the sums work.

Some of that helped. It didn’t give me all the time back.

At forty-two, my body has become less willing to negotiate. My knees hurt. My sleep isn’t recovering as it once did. And my blood pressure needs attention, rather than another promise that I’ll deal with it when things settle down.

So I’m relieved to be stopping.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved, which is an absurd thing to feel and apparently no obstacle to feeling it.

Nobody has accused me of abandoning them. I would tell any colleague making this decision that they were being sensible. I would mean it. I’m trying to extend myself the same courtesy, with mixed results.

***

I drove home on Sunday down the London Road as the sun was coming up. I had the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up, which is how I listen to it: at the wrong time, nowhere near a boat.

The light was coming into the road, and I realised I wouldn’t see it from this side of a night shift again.

I’ll see plenty of early mornings. I know that. But I won’t be driving home from majors with the whole night still in my head, watching the day begin for everyone else.

I was sadder about this than I expected. Also tired, hungry, and pleased that I could go to bed. All of those things were true on the same stretch of road.

I’m not going to find a tidier conclusion than that. Nights gave me friendships, confidence, memories I’m glad to have, and a few I wish I didn’t. They took sleep, time with my family, and more from my health than I wanted to acknowledge. I can be grateful for those years without wanting another fourteen of them.

This week I’ll be learning how to belong entirely to the daytime department. Presumably there will be emails.

And at four in the morning, while I’m hopefully asleep, someone will put bread in the toaster. Someone else will smell it from the corridor and remember they’re hungry.

I hope somebody saves Folasade a piece.
